The Short Commentary on the Parātrīśikā,
composed by the eminent Mahāmāheśvara teacher, the illustrious Abhinavagupta. In that light, all lights are fully absorbed, and in that darkness, all darknesses are likewise contained.
I bow to this unsurpassed light, which consists of both brilliance and darkness. || 1 ||
The Trika has been explained in many ways within the currents of the authentic scriptures;
however, the *Tantrasāra* of the illustrious Utpaladeva is now being described.
That which is eternally Abhinavagupta, ancient yet renowned—that Heart, through the supreme manifestations, itself flashes forth as the Absolute (anuttara). || 3 ||

In that context, it is the deity who is one's own self (*svātmadevatā*) who, in the state of awakening, asks her own self as it descends through the process of reflective awareness (*parāmarśa*). Therefore, it is said: "The Holy Goddess said. What does she ask? To this he replies:
O Lord, tell me the unsurpassed discourse that bestows the Kaulika siddhi by its mere understanding, through which one attains equality with the Khecarī. || 1 ||

O God, whose nature is one's own self (*svātmarūpa*), you are first present everywhere in both cognition and the instruments of action; thus, your form is *anuttara*—meaning unsurpassed, supreme, and transcendent—and in relation to the insentient, it is the nature of the grasper (*grāhaka*). However, for that conscious self (*cidātman*) which is self-luminous, there exists no other grasper.
Supremacy. (p.

2) Therefore, the unsurpassed nature of consciousness, which is always and everywhere manifest, devoid of prior or posterior space and time, and incapable of being denied—what more need be said of it? But this [is as follows]:

To this it is replied: how, indeed, and in what manner does that [Śakti] grant the accomplishment (*siddhi*)—that is, the manifestation through the perceptibility of both sense organs—of the unprecedented form of the *kaulika*, the aggregate of the *kula* consisting of the body, senses, worlds, and so forth, by its own inherent autonomy? This is based on the verbal roots *dā* in the sense of "giving" and *do* in the sense of "cutting."

The meaning is that it emits and withdraws by way of the *dhātus* and *gatis*. Being of the nature of supreme, unitary consciousness (*cit*), how is it that it appears as ever-new—precisely because of this, as the divisible distinctions of the object of knowledge, the act of knowing, and the knower?
Now, what is the point of this? By knowing it in this manner, merely through such knowledge, one attains *khecarī*.

This power of consciousness (*saṃvit-śakti*), while moving through the stages of awakening (*bodha-bhūmi*), should attain, reach, and know equanimity (*samatā*), non-conceptuality (*avikalpatva*), and fullness (*pūrṇatva*) of the Self. However, if its specific nature is not fully understood, it is not *khecarī* (the sky-farer), because it moves within the objective aspect (*vedyāṃśa*) which is of the nature of non-awareness. For that very reason, it is not [considered such] when it is constrained by objects of perception (*vedya*) such as blue and so forth.

[She is] the one whose power is full. Furthermore, since there exist supernatural powers (*siddhis*) produced through the yoga of the vital breath (*prāṇa*) and so forth by means of the sequence beginning with *dhāraṇā*, how can that which is unsurpassed, consisting of pure consciousness (*saṃvinmātra*), and devoid of sequence, bestow the Kaulika-siddhi which possesses sequence, such that by its mere knowledge one would attain the state of being the Goddess? || 1 ||
O Lord, tell me this secret, the great secret:
that power which resides in the heart, Kaulinī, the mistress of the Kula.
Tell that to me, O Lord of Gods, so that I may attain satisfaction; having made this—
which is exceedingly non-manifest, great, supreme, and not secret— self-evident, O Lord, you who possess the power to conceal or reveal your own nature.
He [is the one] for me who am asking about the consciousness of my own self;
"its equality" is an alternative reading.
"But when that mode is not fully known" is another alternative reading.

It has the singular nature of both manifesting and concealing its own essential form; and because it manifests [itself] as the subject (*pramātṛ*), there is an alternative reading: "having the quality of being the source of manifestation.
(p. 3) Speak! Bring [this] to the ultimate state of the continuum of sentences, which is the path of reflective awareness (*vimarśa*). Indeed—

The form of the grasper flashes within the heart of everyone; what need is there for a question regarding that? True, it flashes, yet it has not truly entered the heart. Without entering the heart, even though it appears, it is as if it did not appear at all—like grass or leaves encountered while walking along a street.

For liberation while living (*jīvanmuktatā*) is satisfaction accomplished through the realization of what is heart-pleasing, and for that [satisfaction] which consists of sovereign power (*vibhūti*), satisfaction is accomplished through immersion (*samāveśa*) into that; thus, since this twofold satisfaction does not exist without reflective awareness (*parāmarśa*), the question is indeed appropriate. He demonstrates that very point: "situated in the heart" means residing in the heart, which is the nature of consciousness (*saṃvid*).

She whose power is characterized by absolute freedom (*svātantrya*), for whom the *kula*—the wheel of the grasped, the grasper, and the act of grasping—is the object to be emanated and thus her purpose; she is therefore *Kaulinī*. She is the mistress (*nāyikā*) of that emanated *kula*, its presiding deity (*adhiṣṭhātrī*), the one who causes it to manifest through the awareness of it, and the one who withdraws it back into her own nature. [Give] her to me.

"Speak! Lead me to the path of reflective awareness (*parāmarśa*), so that by being brought to the state of being reflected upon, I may attain satisfaction in the form of both enjoyment (*bhukti*) and liberation (*mukti*). Thus, with the causative suffixes (*ṇic*), he says "speak," meaning "speak in the form of consciousness. In this way, when consciousness, in its state of awakening, [poses] a question—

When she makes the true nature of ultimate reality manifest in its full splendor, then, upon the attainment of the awakened state, she herself becomes the bestower of the response, possessing the full form of the deity Bhairava. And here, this is not a matter of being "for the first time" at all; rather—
That very same ancient [reality], revolving again and again, appears as if it were distinct due to the conceptualization of temporal divisions; thus, it is conventionally designated as "past. || 2 ||
Because it is not perceptible due to its divine form, it is described here as something beyond direct perception.
Śrī Bhairava said:
"Listen, O highly fortunate Goddess, to that which is the unsurpassed answer even to the supreme. (3)
I shall speak of that which undoubtedly bestows the immediate accomplishment of the Kaula,
[reaching] the ultimate limit produced by speech— this is a variant reading.
"The truth flashes forth"— this is another variant reading.
And here, there is also the reading *na cātrecchāṃ prāthamikīṃ kācit*;
and there is also the reading *vedyatvena ca*.
(p. 4) O Goddess, this Kaula method resides within the space of my heart. 4.

O You who possess such a great fortune, characterized by the desire to emerge in the state of awakening—listen and comprehend this clearly! I am that which is the unsurpassed form even of the "higher" subject (*grāhaka*); by the use of the word "even," it includes the object (*grāhya*), the act of grasping (*grahaṇa*), and so forth. I am the bestower of the *kaulika* perfection.

I shall explain that [teaching], whose purpose is the fulfillment of worldly enjoyment (*bhoga*) and liberation (*apavarga*) through the illumination of all things, and I shall lead it to the heart so that, as soon as it is grasped, no further doubt arises. For this Kaulika method, which appears as "this," is...

He, being eternally known as the Heart within the space of my heart, abides as the very nature of consciousness (cidātman), according to such scriptural passages as: "In the beginning, my dear, this was Being alone... (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 6.2.1), "One only, without a second... (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 6.2.1), and "That [Being] thought... (Aitareya Upaniṣad 1.1.1). || 4 ||
And then:
"Now, all the initial lunar days (tithis) end with vowels and the bindu;
within them, through the conjunction of time, the Moon and the Sun are proclaimed. (5)
O virtuous lady, the principles beginning with earth and ending with the Puruṣa are located in sequence within the consonant groups beginning with 'ka' and ending with 'ma'.
There is a tetrad of concentrations (dhāraṇās) on wind, fire, water, and Indra;
above that, the group beginning with Śa is well-known, and before that is the pentad of Brahmā.
O illustrious one, that sequence should be known as rootless; it is declared to be the emanation (sṛṣṭi) of all mantras and vidyās.
1. "Mahānubhavaikaprabuddhā" is an alternative reading.
2. "Yato'hamukrasya" is an alternative reading.
3. "Viśvāvabhāsakādibhogā" is an alternative reading.
(p. 5) This source has been declared at all times in all tantras.

Here, first of all, perception is well known as the illumination of the categories of existence (*padārtha*); and the category of existence consists of the nature of the knower and the knowable. Among these, what is called "the state of being a knower" is characterized by the opening and closing [of the eyes].

By its very nature, characterized by the contraction and expansion of knowledge and action, it has as its essence its own vibration and is not static. Furthermore, how could there be a connection with contraction and expansion for something like a jar, which is limited and insentient in form?
Just as the triangle becomes increasingly manifest within the vibrations of the heart and so forth, so too [does it manifest].
The state of being the knower (*jñātṛtva*) is elevated. To the extent that [this state] diminishes within consciousness as if it were external, to that same extent it is degraded.

Even down to inert objects such as stones, the emission (*visarga*)—characterized by its own contraction and expansion—is the power of the Supreme Lord, whose nature is absolute freedom (*svātantrya*). By that [power],...

The *Rudrayāmala* is said to be the essential nature of Śiva and Śakti, arising from the repose of the union of Bhairava. In the very midst of the conjunction of contraction and expansion lies the Absolute (*anuttara*), Bliss (*ānanda*), Will (*icchā*), Sovereignty (*īśanā*), Expansion (*unmeṣa*), and Diminution (*ūnatā*). From the union of Will and Sovereignty arises the manifestation of the object of knowledge, both indistinct and distinct: *ṛ*, *ṝ*, *ḷ*, *ḹ*.
Because those two, desire (*icchā*) and sovereignty (*īśana*), are joined with the unsurpassed [powers] by means of those very [powers], *ai* arises;
and because expansion (*unmeṣa*) and contraction (*nimeṣa*) are likewise made by those same [powers], *o au* arise.

Immediately thereafter, the entire class of objects of knowledge (*vedya-jāta*) exists in the form of a residual impression (*saṃskāra-śeṣatva*) within the nature of the Bindu, which is the essence of the knower (*vedaka*). In this manner...

It becomes complete; thus, the union of the Supreme Bhairava (parabhairavayāmala) consists of the power of emission (visargaśakti), which is the nature of consciousness as full bliss (pūrṇānandacidrūpa). In that state, the nature of emission is a universal form;
it is not to be counted separately among the fifteen particulars. Such is the Kaulika rule for me.
Abiding in the heart through identity with the nature of consciousness (*saṃvid-rūpa*), thereupon— by the power of this reflective awareness (*parāmarśa*)—
those [phonemes] beginning with *a* and ending with the *bindu* proceed; that is to say, they emerge as the state of the knower.
2. "He becomes full" (*pūrṇo bhavati*) is also a reading.
3. "The Supreme Bhairava consisting of the power of emission" (*visargaśaktimayaparabhairava*) is an alternative reading.
4. The word "this" (*idam*) is not present in manuscript *ka*.
The vowels (*svarāḥ*): they themselves fulfill the state of that which consists of supreme bliss, and thus are called lunar days (*tithayaḥ*).

In this way, that power of reflective awareness (*vimarśaśaktiḥ*) of the moon of consciousness—the unsurpassed (*anuttara*) which consists of the bliss of light—is fulfilled by means of the fifteen lunar days. And all these vowels have the nature of sounding (*śabdana*).

The ultimate selves (*paramārthātmānaḥ*), shining by themselves in relation to the world, are self-luminous. Within them are the moon and the sun, which represent contraction and expansion; they consist of that, and within them is that—namely, the emission (*visarga*) consisting of the two points (*bindu*). Therefore, through Time, which consists of synthesis, [all these are unified] within all of these.

The yoga of reflective awareness (*parāmarśana-yoga*). For that reason, reflective awareness is indeed of the nature of vibration (*spandana*), and not of a fixed, immobile, and inert form. Even externally, the moon and sun move within the fifteen lunar days (*tithi*) by way of the contraction and expansion of night and day. This...

That is the Blessed Lady, the power of supreme reflection (*parāmarśa-śakti*). And that very manifestation of the object of knowledge (*vedya-ullāsa*) which exists within Will (*icchā*) and Lordship (*īśana*), becoming differentiated, consists of ten principles (*tattva*): as grossness, it is the nature of the five elements (*bhūta-pañcaka*), and as subtlety, it is the nature of the five subtle elements (*tanmātra-pañcaka*). [These are] earth, water, fire, air, ether, and smell...

Taste, form, touch, and sound— this very radiance of the object of cognition (*vedya-ullāsa*), being projected as instruments, constitutes the sense organs (*indriya*). Among these, the organs of action (*karmendriya*)—

namely the genitals, anus, feet, hands, and speech— are characterized primarily by the power of action (*kriyā-śakti*), while those characterized primarily by the power of knowledge (*jñāna-śakti*) are the [organs of perception].

The organs of perception (buddhīndriyas) are the nose, tongue, eye, skin, and ear. Then, through the gradual manifestation of the appearance of experience within the cycle of transmigration (saṃsāra), there arise the mind (manas), ego (ahaṃkāra), intellect (buddhi), primordial matter (pradhāna), and the person (puruṣa).
Likewise, the elements beginning with earth and ending with the person are contained within the letters from *ka* to *ma*. And as for the person (*puruṣa*)...
The enumeration of the aggregate of objects of knowledge (*vedyarāśi*) occurs precisely upon that which has the nature of being known (*saṃvedyarūpa*) and terminates in the letter *ma*.

For without that, how could earth and the other elements be objects of knowledge? Therefore, this is the form of the manifestation of the object of knowledge itself, which belongs to the aggregate of objects of knowledge that has not abandoned its status as an object of knowledge, yet is distinct—
1. *Paramārthātmanaḥ* is an alternative reading.
2. *Tithipañcadaśakasyāntaścarantaḥ* is an alternative reading.
3. *Jñānaśaktiprādhānyāni* is an alternative reading.
4. There is also a reading: "of that which consists of the object of cognition (*saṃvedya*) itself and is limited.

5. There is another reading: "this is not the form of the manifestation of the object of cognition alone. (p. 7) The unification of the cognized and the cognizer. The principles (*tattva*) excluded from that [unification]. The *kalās* are of the nature of air; they are something slight...
As the impeller by means of agency, impure *vidyā* is of the nature of light and illuminates through limited knowledge.
*Māyā* is of the nature of water, characterized by the paralysis consisting of immersion in the form of attachment.
The power of passion (*rāga-śakti*) is of the nature of earth, indicated by Indra. These four powers [bind] the person.

They hold [the world] in their midst without resting upon it, like Triśaṅku; otherwise, they would either fall onto the dull ground like stones and other such things, or else fall into the sky of consciousness like the Supreme Lord. In both cases, in the absence of the state of being a subject under *māyā*, there would be no object of knowledge whatsoever, and neither contraction nor expansion would exist.

Because expansion is impossible without contraction, all this is implied by that [consciousness] in the form of emission (*visarga*), which consists of both contraction and expansion— namely, the creation of the object (*vedya*) and the corresponding creation of the subject (*vedaka*). However,
there is no need here for the power of space (*ākāśa-śakti*) to establish the state of the subject of *māyā* (*māyā-pramātṛtā*), for she [the power of space]...
Inherent within the Person (puruṣa), due to the emptiness of the object of knowledge and because it can tolerate the space for objects of knowledge,

there exists his own eternal power of reflective awareness (vimarśa-śakti) by virtue of his being the subject (pramātṛ). However, when there is a gradual concealment of the state of being an object and the manifestation of the nature of consciousness, therein lies "sustenance" (dhṛti), which is of that very same nature.

Nourishment (*āpyāyana*) is the conjunction with its manifestation. In that very state, vibration (*spandana*), which consists in the attainment of supreme sovereignty, pervades everything in that same form. Thus, this pentad beginning with *Ś* is the nourisher, the fulfiller, and the pervader of one's own nature.
It is characterized by Vidyeśvara, Sadāśiva, Śakti, and Śiva;
it consists of the subtle forms of earth, water, fire, air, and ether;
and it takes the form of Sadyojāta, Vāmadeva, Aghora, Tatpuruṣa, and Īśāna.
It is designated by the term "the fivefold Brahman. Thus, this is the emission-power (*visarga-śakti*), which possesses both transcendent (*parā*) and immanent (*aparā*) forms.
And that fivefold form, being of such a nature, again rests within the Absolute (*anuttara*). In this way, it is indeed the emission-power itself, which is primordial.
1. "They cause [them] to rest" is an alternative reading.
2. "Because even expansion is absent" is an alternative reading.
3. "And the creation of the object of knowledge" is an alternative reading.
4. An alternative reading is *ākāśaśaktyātmeti*. 5. An alternative reading is *vedyatveti*. 6. An alternative reading is *pramātṛrūpatvāditi*.
7. "In the form of the venerable Parāpara" is an alternative reading.
8. "The power of reflective awareness (vimarśaśaktiḥ)" is an alternative reading.
9. "In the form of the five elements (bhūtapañcakarūpam)" is an alternative reading.
Likewise, there is also a reading "consisting of the power of reflective awareness" (*vimarśaśaktimaya*).

From this point up to the end of the passage ending with "the fivefold Brahman," [the reality] unfolds in this very form. This is the wheel of powers (*śakticakra*) of the Lord Bhairavanātha, which exists as an uninterrupted continuity.
For indeed, the powers of the upward movement (*unmeṣa*), the downward movement (*icchā*), the triangle (*trikoṇa*), and emission (*visarga*)—
which possess fivefold differentiation— are the powers of consciousness (*cit*), bliss (*ānanda*), will (*icchā*), knowledge (*jñāna*), and action (*kriyā*),
consisting of the five powers that constitute the objective world (*vācyabhūta*). And therefore:
All this, first of all, consists of the nature of non-differentiated awareness;

then, through the nature of differentiated awareness, it takes on the form of the fifty-fold awareness. However, when it attains the status of an object (*karmatā*) in the form of that which is to be perceived, the external web of principles (*tattva-jāla*) arises. Its very life-force is its nature as awareness.

And she is in the form of the *mātṛkā*. For this very reason, she is the [source] of all mantras that possess secret meanings— consisting of seed-syllables (*bīja*) and clusters (*piṇḍa*), such as those of four or nine kalās—
and of the *vidyās* which are determined by the denotations of masculine forms.

This is the source— the cause consisting of the form of non-dual reflective awareness— of all the *mālā-mantras* such as "namaḥ śivāya," whose forms have clearly manifest meanings being experienced, and of all those [mantras] determined to have feminine designations; this is taught in all the secret Tantras, beginning with the Śiva and Rudra Tantras.

Whatever is spoken, all of that arises from this very source. Indeed, every form that bestows the attainment of both the supreme and the lower is found within the thirty-six principles (*tattva*). And of that [system], its life-force is the state of being the perceiver of its insentient form—which serves as the locus of the body—and that [life-force] resides in this [thirty-sixfold system].
"In the Bhagavatī" means that she alone bestows all this. For this very reason, the Bhagavatī possesses the nature of the questioner here.

It is well known as "Yaśasvinī" precisely because of her heart-captivating quality. She is addressed as "Yaśasvinī" because she has become renowned as the form of the universal self (*viśvātmarūpa*) to this extent. And she is that threefold emanation whose root is the syllable *A*.

Those ending with the letter *kṣa* are of unsurpassed form; their manifestation, moreover, occurs through the door of rest within the very self of Śiva— as for "vimarśaśaktayaḥ," there is an alternative reading.
2. "Possessing the fivefold division" is an alternative reading.
3. "Having attained the state of being subsequent" is an alternative reading.
4. "Residing within the nature of the seed" is an alternative reading.
5. "Whatever it may be" (*yatkiṃcit*) is an alternative reading. 6. "The form of the non-establishment of the other" (*parāsiddhirūpam*) is an alternative reading.
7. "Thirty" (*triṃśat*) is an alternative reading.
8. *prasiddham*—this is an alternative reading.
9. *anuttararūpāt prabhṛti*—this is an alternative reading.
10. *śivātmany evānuttaradhāmni*—this is an alternative reading.

She who finds rest in that very same unsurpassed abode is described as being such; she should be known as the Real (satī). Through her recognition, that nature of the unsurpassed vibration is thoroughly understood—namely, that which is called "the unsurpassed" (anuttara). Thus, she resides in the heart.

It has been determined in the Śivarudrarahasya and other Tantras that the power (śakti), which was previously of the nature of non-discriminative awareness, attains the state of discriminative awareness— the form of Kaulika perfection— precisely through this sovereignty of the unsurpassed (anuttara) nature. || 8 ||

One might object: "But surely, as long as the nature of the Heart—which is the foundation for the distinct perception of divisions despite being essentially indivisible—remains, has doubt not been dispelled? Anticipating this objection, he instructs:
"O Bhadrā, [the letter] joined with the fourteenth and endowed with the end of the lords of the lunar days (tithīśa)."
O lady of beautiful hips, the third Brahma is the heart of the Bhairava-Self.
By means of the fourteenth vowel, which is endowed with the supreme bliss of fullness and possesses the perfection of the unfolding of the body of the complete power of action (*kriyāśakti*),
[the Absolute] is joined with and eternally intermingled with the pair of Will and Knowledge, which are internally dissolved within the gateway of the power of action.
That is to say, this universe— which consists of the third principle, Brahman-Sadāśiva,

which is of the nature of existence and distinct from the aggregate of objects to be grasped— is perfectly endowed with, and rests within, the *visarga* (the emission) that constitutes the end or final limit of the fifteen vowels known as the *tithīśas*.

The heart of the Blessed One, whose nature is Bhairava, who is the mass of sounds (*śabdarāśi*), and whose body is the universe, is its essential core. For just as the term "heart" (*hṛdaya*) is used to denote the abode of rest within the non-dual light and reflective awareness (*prakāśavimarśa*) of that [body]— which consists of all the principles (*tattva*), has a body composed of them, and is governed by the continuous series of distinct elements such as the skin and so forth— in the same way...

This body of the Blessed Lord Bhairavanātha, consisting of the differentiated principles (*tattva*), worlds (*bhuvana*), and so forth, whose essence is reflective awareness (*parāmarśa*) and which consists of the fifty phonemes, is *Śakti*; there is an alternative reading: "that [body] is the differentiation."
2. There is also a reading *parāmarśasya*.
3. The word *satī* does not exist in manuscript *ka*.
4. As it has been said: "In this fourteenth abode, wherein the three powers have become manifest, there is therefore the state of the trident."

The Teacher has stated in the *Śrīpūrvaśāsana*: "That [reality], whose essence is the principle of Sadāśiva, whose nature is the light of Aghora, and which is characterized by the mass of objects to be grasped (grāhyarāśi) consisting of the non-manifest 'this-ness' (idantā). (Note: There is an alternative reading: "...characterized by the mass of objects to be grasped consisting of the manifest 'this-ness' (*sphuṭībhūtedantātmaka*). )
6. "From which certainty" is an alternative reading.
7. "Of the restrained one" is an alternative reading. (p.
10) This heart of his consists of the essence of the non-dual reflective awareness of that [reality]. O Blessed One, O lady of beautiful hips!

This heart is the very essence of Bhairava, whose nature is Bhairava; it consists of the continuous vibration of the triangle, which takes the form of incessant contraction and expansion residing within the three powers of the abode that is supreme bliss and rest.
It is the reality of the venerable Goddess Parā, who is his own self and non-different from him.

Supreme consciousness (*anuttararūpā saṃvit*) is as follows: through the vibration (*parispanda*) of the two initial points of sound (*svarakoṭi*), which are the very essence of the seed-syllable (*bījātman*) resting in its own nature, it consists of all the principles (*tattva*) in the form of emanation (*sṛṣṭi*), by means of a differentiated reflective awareness (*vibhaktaparāmarśātman*) at the central point, solely through the power of that vibration. For this very reason, it will be stated:
"But having encapsulated the emanation," thus [it is said]. || 9 ||
Neither one born of the Yoginīs nor one who is not Rudra clearly attains this Heart of the God of gods, which bestows immediate liberation through yoga. (10)

He who obtains this seed is not a mere animal even at the very moment of its acquisition, because once it is obtained, this Heart arises. This very state of being the Heart is Bhairava-hood. Therefore, as long as the unfolding of the nature of Śakti has not arisen through the union of Rudra and Yoginī, how can this Heart unfold?

When this [reality] has been unveiled, there is union with this very heart. This attainment of the heart—characterized by immersion (*samāveśa*) into the *Śrī Bhairavayāmala*—bestows liberation even while one is living; thus, by its mere unveiling, there is the supreme *kaulikī* perfection characterized by liberation-in-life (*jīvanmuktatā*) within the unsurpassed state whose nature is pure consciousness (*saṃvinmātra*), just as follows:
It is so ordained; thus it has been demonstrated. || 10 ||
Now, that manner in which other accomplishments (*siddhis*) characterized by sovereign power (*vibhūti*) also arise—
by the force of the reflective awareness of the vibration of consciousness (*saṃvit-parispanda*),
independently of any mockery of the vital breath, the channels, time, direction, mantras, *vidyās*, ritual conduct, and so forth— that [manner]...
This reality (tattva) becomes [manifest] through the preliminary approach; this is the reading in manuscript *ka*.
There is an alternative reading: "by means of vibration (*spandena*) at the beginning."
3. "Mayyaiva" is an alternative reading.
4. "Jñāyate" is an alternative reading.
5. "Atha" is an alternative reading.
"6 yojanas" is an alternative reading.
"It causes the unfolding of the heart's light to close" is an alternative reading. (p.

When this [mantra] is properly uttered, the great multitude of mantras and mudrās immediately becomes present before one, characterized by the entry of their power into one's own body.

(p. 21) Even regarding the ritual implements for worship, one should effect identity with the Heart [of the deity] by means of the essence of supreme bliss resting in the *arghya* vessel, having established that identity through the Heart-seed mantra recited twenty-seven times;
then, by sprinkling that essence, one should bring about identity with the Heart. Immediately thereafter, [one should do so] for the support of the worship.

[This refers to] the linga, the sacrificial ground (sthaṇḍila), and so forth. Thus, having dissolved duality in a general sense, having cast off that which is presided over by the body and vital breath, having removed it even from the sacrificial hall where one worships, having set it aside from the articles of worship, the intended meaning is that one should likewise reject it even from the substratum of the worship itself. || 28 ||

When this has been done, he describes the nature of worship, preceded by the conceptualization of the object of worship, within that support of worship— whether it be an external or internal form, or any one of the hundreds of various types such as a *liṅga*, a sacrificial mound (*sthaṇḍila*), or a mandala— which has been selected according to one's preference and as is available.
The preparation of the seat is performed with a flower consecrated fourteen times with the mantra. || 29 ||
There, the hero should worship the emanation (sṛṣṭi), and then again the seat;
having encapsulated the emanation, he should thereafter begin the sacrifice.
One should worship the highly fortunate Goddess, who is perfectly complete in all her principles (tattvas) and adorned with all her limbs, while reciting the twenty-seven mantras.
Then, one should worship with fragrant flowers according to one's ability;
one should honor [the deity] with supreme devotion and offer oneself as well. || 32 ||

Regarding "fourteen": one should conceive of the *āsana* (seat) as that which pervades the fourteen-fold state consisting of the four stages beginning with waking and ending with the fourth (*turya*), which is the body of the seed-syllable ending in the vowel *au*. Thus, the emanation (*sṛṣṭi*) from *a* to *kṣa*, resting in such an *au*-kāra, is embraced by the power of emission (*visarga-śakti*) and remains situated above it.
It is to be cultivated. [The phrase] "in all undifferentiated masses" refers to the body, vital breath, and so forth; this is an alternative reading.
According to the reading in manuscript *ka*, it also refers to "the supports of worship."
3. "By means of form" is an alternative reading.
4. "Having been embraced" is an alternative reading.
5. "From the comprehension of the essential nature of worship" is an alternative reading.
Immediately after the word "rested" (*viśrāntāḥ*), there is the phrase "or by all.
In that state of rest within the activity beyond the fourth (*turyātīta-vṛtti*), that very resting which is emission (*visarga*) is itself the sacrifice (*yāga*).
And even in that emission-phase (*visarga-kalā*) of the activity beyond the fourth, wherein the entire work of emanation has been assumed—
One should worship by adding that very form ending in the vowel *au*, which encompasses the four states beginning with waking;

for the *visarga* situated in its center touches the true state existing at both extremes. Therefore, one should worship her whose nature is the *visarga*, who consists of all the *tattvas*, and who is endowed with the entire multitude of entities acting as her limbs.

He accepts Śrī Parādevī, who exists non-differently from Maheśāna Parabhairava and whose nature is the Absolute (anuttara). This is what is meant: in the foundational part of the Heart, within the objective aspect which consists of the sixfold state (ṣaḍvṛtti).

Having come to rest within that which consists of the three states of waking, dreaming, and deep sleep— characterized by the triad of distinctions as very clear, clear-and-obscure, and obscure— and which always possesses the form of the first digit of pure Being (*sanmātra*), one who has rested sequentially from the end of the principles of *śakti* and *śiva* up to the fourth state (*turya-pada*) in that supreme nature (*anuttara-rūpa*) during the cycle of return;

By the acceptance of all the principles (tattvas) as non-distinct from the sequence, the pervasion of the seat (*āsana*) is demonstrated. Then, as long as the sixteenth digit (*kalā*), which is of the nature of emission (*visarga*) and identical with Bhairava, is touched in its state of transcending everything, so long does everything abide within it non-differently; thus, that seventeenth digit, whose form is the non-duality of all, is precisely that.

The sacrifice is of unsurpassed form; in it, rest is thus set in motion. That alone is the sacrifice in the ultimate sense. However, for the sake of accomplishing that very nature, by means of fragrant flowers—which effortlessly enter the heart—through the very offering of one's own essential nature within the heart, [the goal is attained].

By means of all substances, both internal and external, which nourish the heart according to one's capacity— since that whose power and nature have not been appropriated and whose function is contracted is unfit for sacrifice— one should [perform it] by means of power (*śakti*), which consists of the expansion of one's own nature and is also beneficial through its external, blissful form.
1. "By means of bathing, ointment, incense, and betel"—this is an alternative reading.
2. "Having its own natural function gone"—this is an alternative reading.
3. *Sarvātītarūpām* is also a reading.
4. *Sadvyāptirūpavedyāṃśe* is an alternative reading. 5. Immediately after *tathā*, this additional reading is seen: *tathā pūraṇā (pūrṇā) ata eva*.
"Twenty-seven times" is the reading;
"within the heart" (*hṛdayānte*) is an alternative reading.
One should worship correctly with the power of external substances, made auspicious by the collection of perfumes and other offerings. How so?

By means of supreme devotion— which, by rendering secondary the limited body, vital breath, the subtle body (*puryaṣṭaka*), and so forth, brings about a state of profound humility characterized by immersion into their true nature,
and which is defined by the attainment of primacy in the form of the Supreme Consciousness consisting of the deity to be worshipped as described therein.
The meaning is: "by means of the vessel" refers to that which bestows immersion through an excess of faith; and this is *parā* (supreme) devotion.

One should perceive oneself as being filled by that beautiful and delightful portion—the fragrance—which forcibly enters one's own heart from the flowers and other ritual implements used in the sacrifice.
One should cause [the deity] to be known by means of a rule consisting of the ascertainment of the functioning of all non-differentiated forms; twenty-seven times,
at the moment of utterance,
[one should perceive] that non-differentiated essential nature being filled by various external and internal collections of objects, such as flowers and so forth.

The meaning is that one should repeatedly contemplate the nature of the Self in such a way that one knows the Self to consist of the venerable goddess Parā; this, first of all, is worship in the form of radiant manifestation (*sphuraṇa*). And from that [comes the state] of the Lord Bhairava, the enjoyer, whose nature as the source of all objects of enjoyment has been internalized within his own belly.
Through the oblation (*homa*), which consists of illumination (*uddīpana*),

one must perform a reflective awareness (*parāmarśa*) by means of its power to burn away and dissolve the nature of that which remains as a latent impression (*saṃskāra*) within it, so that— according to the principle of digestion— that impression exists only in the form of a seed.

Furthermore, the fear of the great disease— the birth of the fundamental divisions consisting of latent impressions characterized by re-arising— is pacified, just as in the state of deep sleep. || 32 ||
With this intention, while concluding the sacrifice (*yajana*), he indicates the fire-oblation (*homa*).
Thus the sacrifice has been explained; this same procedure applies to the fire-ritual (*agnikārya*) as well.
There too, there is the sprinkling (*abhyukṣaṇa*) of the sesame seeds and other materials with water consecrated by reciting the *śikhā-mantra* the prescribed number of times.

The preparation of the seat with flowers consecrated fourteen times by reciting [the mantra] over the *sruk* and *sruva* ladles and other implements in the fire, up to the point of the "encasement" (*saṃpuṭīkaraṇa*), constitutes the offering to the deity to be worshipped. Then—[regarding the word *tataḥ*], there is an alternative reading:
*tati-sadya*, meaning "immediately thereafter" or "with excellence."
2. *rūpām* is an alternative reading for *vṛttim*.
3. *niyamayet* is an alternative reading.
4. *kṛtvoccāraṇāvasare* is an alternative reading.
5. "Being filled with its own essential nature" (*nijasvarūpa*) is an alternative reading.
6. "In the form of that filling" (*tāvatpūraṇarūpa*) is an alternative reading.
7. "By means of the illustration of the state of deep sleep" (*suṣuptyavasthādṛṣṭāntena*)—or alternatively, "by means of the account of deep sleep" (*suṣuptāvṛttāntena*)—is an alternative reading.
(24) Having offered the oblation of parched grain and so forth in its complete form, one should offer oneself as well;

according to this explained sequence, the offering of the *pūrṇāhuti* constitutes the ritual procedure for the fire-sacrifice (*agnikārya*). Thus, the essential nature of worship consists indeed in the full integration of both sacrifice (*yāga*) and oblation (*homa*).

To this extent, the supreme Goddess Śrī Bhagavatī, whose nature is one's own self, becomes perfectly worshipped; for as long as the dissolution of internal impurity has not occurred, the state of being composed of manifest consciousness is not fulfilled. Therefore, this is indeed worship by means of the cessation of internal conceptualization.
By this, he says that by gathering external substances, one who has properly performed the ritual of worship attains success through the correct recollection of the seed-syllable. || 33 ||
One should meditate upon the seed-syllable, devoid of beginning and end, blooming in the midst of the lunar days, situated within the heart-lotus; one should practice this constantly. (34)

"Properly" means having performed the ritual of worship in the manner described; and "properly" also means remembering and contemplating the seed-syllable (*bīja*) according to the direction of the instructions already stated and those yet to be stated. Thus, he attains perfection properly; by this very body, he becomes a vessel for all sovereign powers, just like the deity Parabhairava. Of this...
Because the heart's reflective awareness, appearing in ever-new forms,

does not correctly manifest as prior or even more prior states, the temporal distinctions that would otherwise apply are cast aside; thus, the object of manifestation is in every respect entirely internal.

Because it manifests what exists, because it resembles the nature of recollection, because it is designated as "recollection," and because the suffix *śatṛ* indicates a present state that is non-different from the past— this is what is indicated.
Thus, this reflective awareness (*parāmarśa*) must be accepted as being devoid of any interruption.

He becomes one whose nature is eternally manifest and who is not limited by time. Regarding what was said—"remembering perfectly"—although that "perfection" (*samyaktva*) has been shown previously [in the passage] "for it is full, consisting of union," etc., [it is explained here]. (Note: *Melanātmaka* is provided as a variant reading for *melanātmaka*.)
2. "Of that which is latent" (antarlīnasya) is the reading in manuscript K.
3. "Dissolved" (vigalitam) is another reading in manuscript K.
4. "As long as it is not the nature of one's own self" (yāvatsvātmarūpaṃ na) is another reading.
5. "Always within, as if a secret"—this is an alternative reading. 6. "Devoid of division"—this is an alternative reading.
(p. 25) Beginning from the Fire of Time (Kālāgni)... (verse 21).

With this extensive passage, he further clarifies what has been determined in a clear manner by stating: "devoid of beginning and end. The seed (*bīja*) is the form of the signifier (*vācaka*); the heart (*hṛdaya*) is its signified (*vācya*), which is the lunar portion (*somāṃśa*).
This is the *yāmala*—the mass of light arising from the union—of the Lord Bhairavanātha together with his Śakti.

The instruction is that one should practice through the process of identifying the signified (*vācya*) with the signifier (*vācaka*). However, in the reading *somāṃśam*, it refers to that which consists of the moon of perfect knowledge, whose ultimate reality is light and bliss.

Precisely from that [source], there arises the manifestation and withdrawal of the universe, demonstrated by the power of contraction and expansion through the essential activity of blazing and melting.

The Great Heart, which is of the nature of a triangle and unsurpassed, is permeated by three parts characterized by the letters *sa*, *au*, and *aḥ*—which constitute a progressively higher [manifestation] rooted in the power of unimpeded accomplishment (*sampādanāpratihatasāmarthya*). And its three parts are its constituent portions (*aṃśa*); thus, in a collective sense, there is "Soma" and "Aṃśa."

This pair— this very tetrad— having come face-to-face and come to rest within the Heart whose nature is self-awareness, should be cast into the culmination of immersion (*samāveśa*) by means of an identity that encompasses everything down to the levels of intellect, vital breath, and body; it should be characterized primarily by the reflective awareness of that [nature], with its state of insentience dissolved, and having as its sole essence the support of that [awareness].
The entire aggregate consisting of intellect, vital breath, body, senses, and so forth, is the *kula*;
by virtue of the expansion that reveals its own form within that [reality], one should cause it to attain the state of the *prakāśakula*.
Thus, the instruction regarding the fourfold emission (*visarga*) is shown by this. In that regard, first, the primary [emission] is as follows:

He describes the nature of the Full Heart (Pūrṇahṛdaya): that which is devoid of beginning and end—that is, free from origination and destruction—is the seed of the universe. Precisely because it is the seed, it expands as the soul of the universe, undergoing incessant unfolding;
it stands at the center of the lunar days (tithis), which are the forms of time for the universe, by way of its universal form.

One should constantly meditate upon that consciousness, which exists within one's own heart characterized by consciousness as a lotus due to its engagement in the play of contraction and expansion; having entered that consciousness, one should cause it to blossom by forcibly dispelling its contraction. And therefore:

The accomplishment of the state of Pūrṇabhairava [is attained] with respect to both the arising and the recitation. "The beginning and the end consist of vowels and consonants. Alternatively, there is another reading: "That seed-syllable which is devoid of those [vowels and consonants] is itself [the goal]."
"2vihṛhya" is an alternative reading.
Since it consists of the *visarga* and from it the other fifteen lunar days (*tithi*) blossom, it resides in the midst of all lunar days. One should meditate upon that in the heart-lotus as before.

Having the form of the mere movement of the trident, expanding within the lunar days (*tithi*) and the currents of the *prāṇa* and *apāna*, situated in the center, and effecting immersion into that nature of the vital breath (*prāṇa*), one should meditate on it in the heart in the form of a seed-syllable as it enters the body through that gateway. The letters are situated in the *ava*-group; the vowels are the first, and "end" refers to that which is at the end—by means of the conjunction with time (*kālayoga*).

Thus, the *visarga* has been described here; therefore, one should meditate upon the seed-syllable (*bīja*)—which is devoid of vowels and *visarga*, consisting of the true activity of the unstruck sound (*anacka-sad-vṛtti*)—situated in the center of the body within the heart, amidst the expanding energies of the *prāṇa* and *apāna*. || 34 ||
Regarding this, he states the result:
"Whatever desires one may desire, one shall quickly attain them all;
the ignorant man attains direct perception [of reality], and omniscience follows—of this there is no doubt. (35)
Thus is the attainment of the fruit of mantra; this is the Rudrayāmala.
For one who practices this, success is achieved and one shall attain omniscience. || 36 ||

These accomplishments (*siddhis*) have indeed been mentioned: in the passage beginning with "among these, starting from Kālāgni" and continuing with "he who remembers [it] quickly for a moment," and "from this he attains direct perception and omniscience," accomplishment is said to occur in merely three *praharas*. However, regarding immersion (*samāveśa*) through the division of four *praharas*:

When everything has indeed become luminous and attained the state of day, and the contraction of night has waned, one becomes omniscient like Bhairava with this very body. He concludes this as follows: "In this way"—the variant reading is "of all seeds."
2 *Vikasatsu* is an alternative reading. 3 Regarding that, it is the reading in manuscript Ka.
4 *Yāti* is an alternative reading.
"5muhūrtādīnām" is an alternative reading.
"6agneḥ pratyakṣatām" is an alternative reading.
One should perform the reflective awareness (*parāmarśa*) of the fire that consumes and dissolves the nature of specific objects of enjoyment.
The immersion into the portion of emission (*visarga*).

(p. 27) Since the fruits of mantra—which consist of the accomplishments (*siddhi*) of both the supreme (*parā*) and the non-supreme (*aparā*)—are obtained from this very unsurpassed seed-syllable (*anuttarabīja*), for this reason, it is precisely this [which is the cause].

Because it brings about the fruit of the *rudrayāmala*— which consists of ten million and a quarter [verses]— it is called the *rudrayāmala*, owing to the eternal union (*nityasaṃghaṭṭa*) of Śiva and Śakti herein. For this very reason, he states that the fruit for one who practices this, in brief, is the attainment of the nature of Bhairava, characterized by omniscience and omnipotence.
"For one practicing this...
[as stated]. However, even without such practice, there is supreme liberation while living (*jīvanmuktatā*), which is the *kaulikī-siddhi*; may there be auspiciousness! (36)
That which was previously fragmented and scattered has been well-preserved here in the terminology of the Tantra;
that supreme reality has been elucidated herein by Abhinavagupta. (1)
May those devoted to this discernment not become vessels for delusion;
may these true disciples attain, this very day, the perfection of the state of Bhairavī.
They are those who know the complete security and well-being of unsurpassed bliss,
and who are skilled in the immersion that swallows up the three worlds.
I salute this supreme consciousness, in which [all things] are eternally full by virtue of its nature as Will, Knowledge, and Action, and from which these [phenomena] are emitted.
1. "Mantrakalānām" is an alternative reading.
2. "Kaulikīsiddhiḥ parāparāṇām" is also a reading.
3. "Bhāṣitam" is also a reading.
"4 *bhājanāḥ* is an alternative reading.
5 *prāpnuyād eva* is also a reading.
6 *abhijāyatām* is an alternative reading."
The God Maheśvara, who is concealed by that power of ever-new forms— that which is the stainless nature of both— is [the object of worship].
I salute Śiva, who is Abhinavagupta. || 5 ||
This *Parātrīśikā-laghuvṛtti*, titled *Anuttara-tattva-vimarśinī*, composed by one who attained renown through meditating upon the lotus-feet of the Three-eyed Lord, is completed.
This is the work of Bhinavaguptapāda; may there be auspiciousness.
